title: Ashtpadi 11, salok: the doer of all
hookLine: karan kaaran prabh ek hai: He alone is the doer and the cause

cards: Watch a toddler with a toy steering wheel in the back seat of a car. He turns it hard left; the car happens to turn left. He shouts with delight.
He's sure he did that. He turns it right; the car goes straight. He turns harder.
Still straight. Frustration. The grown-ups laugh, because they can see who's actually driving.

Then they go back to gripping wheels of their own: the plan, the career, the children's futures, sure that every turn of the road is theirs. The eleventh salok is a short, gentle word about the real driver.

teach.h: KARAN: THE DOING. KAARAN: THE CAUSE.
teach.b: The salok has two lines. The first: karan kaaran prabh ek hai, doosar naahee koe. God alone is the doer and the cause of causes; there is no other.
Karan is doing, the deed. Kaaran is the cause, the reason behind the deed. Karan kaaran: the one who does, and the cause behind every cause.
Doosar naahee koe: there's no second.
The second line: Nanak is a sacrifice to Him, who is in the water, on the land, and in the sky. Balihaar is the word for giving oneself up in love, being a sacrifice to someone.
So a line that could sound like cold philosophy, one cause of everything, ends in love, and in a God found everywhere. Now, a careful point. Sikh teaching doesn't say our choices don't matter.
Japji says plainly that we ourselves sow and we ourselves eat what we sow. Sikhs are asked to work hard, earn honestly and act. What the salok takes away is not the effort.
It's the illusion that we're the only ones driving.

teach.h: YOUR PART, NOT THE WHOLE ROAD.
teach.b: You can turn your wheel with all your heart; you just stop believing the whole road answers to you.
That's the peace the salok points to: doing your part fully, and leaving the outcome with the doer of all.

how: Sikhs read this salok at the opening of Sukhmani's eleventh ashtpadi, and teachers draw on 'karan kaaran' to describe working wholeheartedly while trusting the outcome to Waheguru.

o: the doer, and the cause of every cause
a vow to do your duty well
a prayer said before starting work

games.q: the eleventh salok — tap the pairs.
p: a sacrifice, given up in love

s: the salok says human choices don't matter
Japji says we sow and eat what we sow; the salok removes the illusion that we drive the whole road.
the salok finds God in water, land and sky
Nanak is a sacrifice to Him who is everywhere.
karan kaaran means the doer and the cause of causes
the one who does, and makes things be done.

games.q: you've worked hard for something and done your part. by the eleventh salok, what now?
o: grip harder until it turns out right.
leave the outcome with the doer of all.
games.why: karan kaaran prabh ek hai: do your part fully, and stop believing the whole road answers to you.

practice: Think of an outcome you're gripping right now, an interview, a diagnosis, a child's choice, and honestly name your part in it and whether you've done it.
Then picture your hands on that toy steering wheel, feel how tight they are, and loosen them, finger by finger, on the out-breath; you're still in the car, and you still care where it goes.
If you pray, you can place the outcome with the doer of all.

wordCard.voice: Karan kaaran, the doer and the cause of causes. The salok says God alone is this, found in water, land and sky.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: karan kaaran, the doer and the cause of causes; the eleventh salok's name for God.

carryVoice: Your line: he is the doer. Your part, done fully, and the road left to him. Day four hundred seventy-eight, done.

sources.work: Guru Granth Sahib (Guru Arjan, Gauri Sukhmani)
